messages.subject: [statnet_help] Help understanding estimation routine
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I want to make sure I understand the machinery underlying ergm. Here's what
I think I understand: For each iteration there's an initial guess at
parameter values, usually from MPLE to start or from the previous
iteration. Those parameters are used to accept or reject edge-toggle
proposals, and the networks from accepted toggles are used to generate a
sample of the sufficient statistics. Then somehow the old parameter values
and the sample of statistics are used to get new parameter estimates. How
does that last step happen, and where do p-values on the parameter
estimates come from? Thanks very much,

Michael



Michael Levy
PhD Candidate
Department of Environmental Science and Policy
University of California, Davis
malevy@ucdavis.edu

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Help understanding estimation routine
messages.body_plain:
Michael,

Sorry for the delay responding.  I needed to check a few things, and 
that sent me off on a longish search.

First, what you describe is right.

The final steps after "somehow" is:

* The MCMC sample of networks is summarized into a matrix of simulated 
sufficient statistics (the network terms in the model) -- with one row for 
each network in the sample from this parameter set

* These are compared to the statistics in the observed network (or the 
target stats, if you're working with egocentric data)

* The resulting deviations are used to solve for the change in the 
parameters that maximizes the estimated likelihood -- the method used to 
solve depends on the erg model; with no curved terms, it uses the 
lognormal approximation and a Nelder-Mead algorithm.

But there's quite a bit of algorithmic detail that has been added over the 
years to make this part of the estimation more efficient.  the most 
important recent change was the adoption of a "steplength" algorithm 
(described here: Hummel RM, Hunter DR, Handcock MS. Improving 
Simulation-Based Algorithms for Fitting ERGMs. Journal of Computational 
and Graphical Statistics. 2012;21(4):920-39. doi: 
10.1080/10618600.2012.679224. PubMed PMID: WOS:000313311100006.) 
Essentially, this takes bigger steps when farther away, and smaller steps 
when close.

* The s.e.'s are calculated from the inverse Hessian matrix at the end.

We made a diagram of the algorithm about a year ago.  See if you can view 
it here:

https://statnet.csde.washington.edu/trac/raw-attachment/wiki/ESS/ergm%20ESS%20flowchart.pdf

If you can't I'll make a pdf and send it to you.

Hope this helps.

> Recent changes in the ergm estimation algorithm mean that these plots

Why is this the case, and where can I read more about this? Does it mean

from the estimated ergm?

Thanks for any help!
Best regards, Christian

messages.subject: [statnet_help] What is the sample returned by ergm() ?
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] What is the sample returned by ergm() ?
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Christian -

That is correct: these statistics are from the sample used to _estimate_ 
the final model, but are not from the final model itself.  As such, they 
are good for general MCMC diagnostics (e.g., is the chain mixing), but 
they will normally understate the degree of convergence of the 
parameters to the MLE.  (In particular, the mean stats for the sample 
will often show greater deviation from the target stats than will the 
expected statistics under the final estimates.)

My sense is that the current consensus among the statnet team is that 
assessment of target stat convergence should be performed as part of 
model adequacy checking using gof(), which usually employs a 
higher-quality MCMC sample than is needed for parameter estimation and 
which can allow assessment of other stats at the same time.  If gof() 
shows poor convergence to the in-model statistics, then refinement of 
the initial ergm() solution is obviously in order; in my experience, 
however, the current code usually does a pretty good job.  Making 
calculation of in-model statistics part of the default behavior for 
gof() (it has always been available, but optional) is in the works, but 
hasn't been rolled out yet.

Pavel or the others may want to chime in further on this issue, but 
that's my understanding of the current state of play.....

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] What is the sample returned by ergm() ?
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] What is the sample returned by ergm() ?
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Christian -

I agree that verifying convergence by the first-order condition is 
always a good idea, and using a full gof run at default settings can be 
overkill when you just need a basic convergence check.  As you suggest, 
one alternative is just to change the settings to get a more modest 
run.  Another approach would be to use the final ergm() sample as an 
importance sample, and obtain an estimate of t(Y)|theta_fin that way.  
You are familiar with this route, but for any home viewers, here's a 
sketch of one approach:

1. Let q0 be the penultimate estimate of theta used to draw the final 
sample, and let q be the final theta of interest.  We have (from ergm()) 
a sample of simulated statistics from t(Y)|q0, which we will call 
t_1,...,t_n for brevity.  Our goal is to estimate E_q t(Y), using our 
sample.

2. Note that 1/n sum_i t_i W(t_i,q,q0) -> E_q t(Y) as n->inf, where 
W(t_i,q,q0) = Pr(t_i|q)/Pr(t_i|q0) is an importance weight.  For our 
case, W(t_i,q,q0) = exp(t * (q-q0)) z(q0)/z(q), where z is the 
normalizing factor (and * is the inner product).  The challenge is 
obviously to calculate z(q0)/z(q).

3. To get the ratio of normalizing factors, we use a similar trick, 
observing that 1/n sum_i exp(t * (q-q0)) -> z(q)/z(q0) as n->inf.

4. Putting this together (and canceling terms), we estimate the target 
mean by
       sum_i t_i exp(t_i * (q-q0)) /[ sum_j exp(t_j * (q-q0)) ]

5. If desired, the Var_q t(Y) can be estimated by estimating E_q t(Y)^2 
and working from there, and the SEs of the estimator itself can be 
estimated by bootstrap or the like.

This takes a few lines of R code, and is quite fast.  Of course, it is 
only accurate when q is close to q0, but that should usually be the case 
here - I haven't done much testing, however, so caveat emptor.  (Also, 
note that this is closely related to how we obtain our final estimates, 
so it may be inclined to err on the side of agreeing with ergm()'s output.)

Others may have alternative suggestions for faster diagnostics, but this 
at least provides one alternative....

-Carter

Pavel or the others may want to chime in further on this issue, but that's my understanding of the current state of play.....

-Carter

Why is this the case, and where can I read more about this? Does it mean that the ...$sample object of the ergm()-result is not a random sample from the estimated ergm?
